specStatements.text: The molecules of a gas are in constant random motion. The temperature of the gas is related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules.
Changing the temperature of a gas, held at constant volume, changes the pressure exerted by the gas.
• explain how the motion of the molecules in a gas is related to both its temperature and its pressure
• explain qualitatively the relation between the temperature of a gas and its pressure at constant volume.
A gas can be compressed or expanded by pressure changes. The pressure produces a net force at right angles to the wall of the gas container (or any surface).
Students should be able to use the particle model to explain how increasing the volume in which a gas is contained, at constant temperature, can lead to a decrease in pressure.
For a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature:
volume, V, in metres cubed, m^3

Students should be able to calculate the change in the pressure of a gas or the volume of a gas (a fixed mass held at constant temperature) when either the pressure or volume is increased or decreased.
Work is the transfer of energy by a force.
Doing work on a gas increases the internal energy of the gas and can cause an increase in the temperature of the gas.
Students should be able to explain how, in a given situation eg a bicycle pump, doing work on an enclosed gas leads to an increase in the temperature of the gas.

scopeNotes.statement: • explain qualitatively the relation between the temperature of a gas and its pressure at constant volume.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification asks for a qualitative explanation only, so this content states the direction of the change and its molecular cause — a higher temperature means a higher average kinetic energy, so molecules strike the walls more often and with greater force, so the pressure rises, and the reverse on cooling. No proportionality between pressure and temperature is stated or implied, no pressure–temperature calculations are set, and the kelvin scale and absolute zero are not introduced here. The only calculations in this section are the ones the specification does require, using pressure × volume = constant at constant temperature.

concepts.definition: The molecules of a gas are in constant random motion. They travel in all directions and at a wide range of speeds, changing direction whenever they collide with each other or with the walls of the container. No molecule keeps one path or one speed for long.

The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its molecules. Raising the temperature raises that average, so the molecules move faster on average. Individual molecules still have a range of speeds; temperature describes the average, not any one molecule.

Gas pressure arises from the collisions of the moving gas molecules with the walls of the container. Each collision exerts a small force on the wall; the huge number of collisions every second adds up to a steady net force spread over the wall area.

A gas is at constant volume when it is sealed in a rigid container that cannot expand or contract, so the space the gas occupies cannot change. Only the temperature and the pressure are free to change.

concepts.term: Pressure and temperature at constant volume
concepts.definition: Changing the temperature of a gas held at constant volume changes the pressure it exerts. Heating raises the average kinetic energy, so the molecules hit the walls more frequently and with more force, and the pressure rises. Cooling has the opposite effect.

concepts.term: Net force at right angles to a surface
concepts.definition: The pressure of a gas produces a net force at right angles to the wall of the gas container, or to any surface in contact with the gas. Molecules arrive from every direction, so the sideways parts of their impacts cancel out and only the component perpendicular to the surface remains.

concepts.term: Compression and expansion of a gas
concepts.definition: A gas can be compressed or expanded by pressure changes. Unlike a solid or a liquid, the molecules of a gas are far apart, so the volume the gas occupies can be squeezed down or allowed to grow when the pressure acting on it changes.

If a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature is given a larger volume, the molecules keep the same average kinetic energy but are spread through a bigger space. Each molecule travels further between wall collisions, so fewer collisions happen each second on each square metre of wall, and the pressure falls.

concepts.term: Fixed mass of gas at constant temperature
concepts.definition: The condition under which pressure × volume = constant holds. The same molecules must stay sealed in the container, with none added or lost, and the temperature must not change. If gas escapes or the temperature changes, the relationship no longer applies.

For a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature, pressure × volume = constant, written as [p V = constant]. Pressure and volume change in opposite directions: doubling the pressure halves the volume, and tripling the volume divides the pressure by three.

The unit of pressure. In the relationship p V = constant the pressure, p, is in pascals, Pa. One pascal is one newton per square metre, so a pressure is a force spread over an area, not a force on its own.

The unit of volume used in this relationship: volume, V, in metres cubed, m^3. Volumes quoted in cubic centimetres or in litres must be converted to m^3 before they are used alongside pressures in pascals.

concepts.term: Using p V = constant in a calculation
concepts.definition: Because p V has the same value before and after the change, the initial pressure × the initial volume equals the final pressure × the final volume. Multiply the two quantities you know together, then divide by the third to find the missing pressure or the missing volume.
Work is the transfer of energy by a force. When a force moves something, energy is transferred from one store to another, and the amount of energy transferred is the work done.

The energy stored by the molecules of a gas, made up of the kinetic energy of their motion and the potential energy of their positions. Doing work on a gas increases the internal energy of the gas and can cause an increase in the temperature of the gas.

concepts.term: Doing work on an enclosed gas
concepts.definition: When a force pushes a piston into a sealed gas, the piston moves while pushing on the gas, so work is done on the gas. That transfer increases the internal energy of the gas, which can raise its temperature — this is why the barrel of a bicycle pump becomes warm in use.

misconceptions.question: A sealed rigid can of gas is warmed. Why does the pressure inside it rise?
misconceptions.correct: The molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster, so they strike the walls more often and each strike exerts a greater force.
misconceptions.misconception: The molecules themselves swell up when the gas is heated, and the bigger molecules press harder on the walls.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet thermal expansion of solids and liquids first and carry 'heating makes things bigger' down to the particle scale. Diagrams that draw hot gas particles as larger circles reinforce it.
misconceptions.correction: Heating changes how fast the molecules move, not how big they are. The size of a molecule does not change with temperature. It is the greater average kinetic energy — faster molecules, more frequent and harder collisions — that raises the pressure.

misconceptions.question: What is the temperature of a gas related to?
misconceptions.correct: The average kinetic energy of the molecules of the gas.
misconceptions.misconception: The total kinetic energy of all the molecules added together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know a large hot object stores more energy than a small one at the same temperature, and conclude that temperature must measure the total. The word 'average' is easy to drop when reciting the statement.
misconceptions.correction: Two containers of the same gas at the same temperature have the same average molecular kinetic energy even if one holds ten times as many molecules and therefore ten times the total energy. Temperature tracks the average, not the total.

misconceptions.question: Do all the molecules in a sample of gas move at the same speed?
misconceptions.correct: No. They move at a wide range of speeds, and each molecule's speed changes at every collision.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes — at a given temperature every molecule moves at the same fixed speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Textbook animations show identical particles bouncing about identically, so 'random' is read as random direction only. The single value implied by 'the temperature' encourages a single value for speed too.
misconceptions.correction: The motion is random in both speed and direction. Collisions constantly redistribute energy, so at any instant some molecules are fast and some are slow. Only the average kinetic energy is fixed by the temperature.

misconceptions.question: In which direction does the net force produced by gas pressure act on a container wall?
misconceptions.correct: At right angles to the wall.
misconceptions.misconception: Along the wall, in the direction the gas is flowing, or at whatever angle the shape of the container suggests.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture a stream of gas blowing past a surface, as in a wind, and transfer that sideways push to a sealed container. Arrows drawn tangentially on diagrams of curved vessels reinforce it.
misconceptions.correction: In a sealed gas the molecules arrive from all directions, so the components of their impacts along the wall cancel. Only the perpendicular components survive, giving a net force at right angles to the wall whatever the shape of the container.

misconceptions.question: Does gas pressure in a sealed container act downwards, like weight?
misconceptions.correct: No. It acts at right angles to every surface the gas touches, including the lid of the container.
misconceptions.misconception: Gas pressure acts downwards, because the weight of the gas presses on the surface below it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Pressure is often introduced with a block resting on a table, where the force really is the weight acting downwards. Students transfer that single-direction picture to gases.
misconceptions.correction: Gas pressure comes from molecular collisions, and these happen on the base, the sides and the lid of a container alike. The weight of the gas is negligible compared with the force from those collisions.

misconceptions.question: A fixed mass of gas expands into a larger volume at constant temperature. Why does the pressure fall?
misconceptions.correct: The molecules travel further between wall collisions, so fewer collisions happen each second on each square metre of wall.
misconceptions.misconception: Each molecule hits the wall more gently, because spreading out makes the molecules lose kinetic energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate 'spread out' with 'weaker' and assume that having more space costs the molecules energy. Constant temperature is stated but is not connected to constant average speed.
misconceptions.correction: At constant temperature the average kinetic energy — and so the force of a typical impact — is unchanged. What changes is the rate of collisions: a bigger space means longer journeys between hits, so the pressure falls.

misconceptions.question: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, how do pressure and volume change together?
misconceptions.correct: In opposite directions, so that pressure × volume keeps the same value.
misconceptions.misconception: In the same direction — doubling the pressure doubles the volume.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most GCSE relationships met before this one are direct proportions, so students default to 'one up, the other up'. The word 'constant' is read as describing the pair rather than their product.
misconceptions.correction: It is the product p V that stays constant, not the ratio. If the pressure doubles the volume must halve to keep the product the same, so pressure and volume always move in opposite directions.

misconceptions.question: A volume is quoted in cubic centimetres. Can it be used directly in p V = constant?
misconceptions.correct: Not as it stands — the specification gives volume, V, in metres cubed, m^3.
misconceptions.misconception: Any volume unit will do, because the units cancel when the two states are compared.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In p1 V1 = p2 V2 the units genuinely do cancel if both volumes use the same unit, so students generalise to cases where they do not, and mix cm^3 with m^3 in one calculation.
misconceptions.correction: Both volumes must be in the same unit, and the specification's unit is metres cubed. Convert every volume to m^3 first — mixing cm^3 and m^3 in one calculation gives an answer wrong by a factor of a million.

misconceptions.question: Does pressure × volume = constant apply to a gas that is being heated?
misconceptions.correct: No. It applies to a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: The pressure of a gas depends only on its temperature, so at constant temperature the pressure stays the same however the volume changes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The relationship is memorised as a formula without its conditions, and those conditions appear in the line above the equation rather than in the equation itself.
misconceptions.correction: The conditions are part of the statement: a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature. Heat the gas, or let some of it escape, and the product p V changes value.

misconceptions.question: Why does the barrel of a bicycle pump become warm when a tyre is inflated?
misconceptions.correct: Work is done on the enclosed gas as it is compressed, raising its internal energy and its temperature, and the gas warms the barrel.
misconceptions.misconception: The warmth comes only from friction between the piston seal and the inside of the barrel.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Friction is the standard explanation for anything that gets warm when it is rubbed or moved, and students can feel the piston sticking, so a familiar cause displaces the unfamiliar one.
misconceptions.correction: Friction contributes a little, but the main effect is that the piston does work on the gas as it compresses it. That transfer increases the internal energy of the gas, so its temperature rises and the barrel warms.

misconceptions.question: What is work?
misconceptions.correct: Work is the transfer of energy by a force.
misconceptions.misconception: Work is a force acting over a distance, or the energy an object stores because it is moving.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The calculation W = F s is met before the definition, so students describe work by its formula. Others confuse work, the transfer, with the kinetic energy store it may fill.
misconceptions.correction: Work names the process of transferring energy, not a force and not a store. A force does work when it moves something, and the energy transferred in that process is the work done.

misconceptions.question: A gas sealed in a pump is compressed quickly and its temperature rises. Where did the energy come from?
misconceptions.correct: From the person pushing the piston, who does work on the gas.
misconceptions.misconception: From warm air drawn in from the surroundings, or from the warmth of the cyclist's hands.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students expect temperature rises to come from heating by a hotter object, because every earlier example of a temperature rise involved a heat source.
misconceptions.correction: No hotter object is needed. Energy is transferred mechanically: the force on the piston moves through a distance, doing work on the gas and increasing its internal energy, which raises its temperature.

misconceptions.question: A gas is heated in a rigid sealed container that cannot change volume. What happens to its pressure?
misconceptions.correct: The pressure rises, because the faster molecules hit the walls more often and harder.
misconceptions.misconception: The pressure stays the same, because the gas is trapped and cannot expand.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students link pressure changes to volume changes only. If nothing can move, they conclude that nothing can change, forgetting that the molecular motion has changed.
misconceptions.correction: Pressure depends on how the molecules move, not only on the space available. Heating raises their average kinetic energy, so collisions with the fixed walls become more frequent and more forceful and the pressure rises.

misconceptions.question: What produces the pressure a gas exerts on its container?
misconceptions.correct: The collisions of the moving molecules with the walls.
misconceptions.misconception: The molecules repel one another and push outwards on the walls.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students who have met electrostatic repulsion look for a force acting between particles at a distance, and 'a gas fills its container' sounds like something is pushing the particles apart.
misconceptions.correction: Gas molecules exert almost no force on each other except during the brief moments they collide. Pressure comes from the impacts themselves — countless collisions each second, each giving the wall a tiny push.

misconceptions.question: What unit is used for the pressure p in p V = constant?
misconceptions.correct: The pascal, Pa.
misconceptions.misconception: The newton, N, because pressure is a push.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Pressure and force are used interchangeably in everyday speech, and pressure is introduced through the force a gas exerts, so the force unit is the one students reach for.
misconceptions.correction: Pressure is force spread over an area, so its unit is not the force unit. The specification gives pressure, p, in pascals, Pa; one pascal is one newton per square metre.

misconceptions.question: What unit is used for the volume V in p V = constant?
misconceptions.correct: Metres cubed, m^3.
misconceptions.misconception: Metres squared, m^2, the unit that appears in the definition of pressure.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Because pressure involves an area in m^2, students carry the squared unit across to the other quantity in the same equation, and 'cubed' and 'squared' are easily swapped under exam pressure.
misconceptions.correction: Volume fills space in three dimensions, so its unit is metres cubed, m^3. The specification states volume, V, in metres cubed; m^2 is an area, not a volume.

misconceptions.question: A gas is compressed and work is done on it. What happens to its internal energy?
misconceptions.correct: The internal energy of the gas increases.
misconceptions.misconception: The internal energy falls, because squeezing the gas forces energy out of it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture squeezing a sponge, where squeezing pushes something out, and they also confuse internal energy with the volume the gas occupies.
misconceptions.correction: Doing work on a gas transfers energy into it, so the internal energy increases and the temperature can rise. Nothing is squeezed out of a sealed gas — the same molecules simply store more energy.

misconceptions.question: Can a gas be compressed?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A gas can be compressed or expanded by pressure changes.
misconceptions.misconception: A gas has a fixed volume that pressure cannot change; only its shape can change.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule learned for liquids — takes the shape of its container, keeps a fixed volume — is over-applied to gases, since both are fluids and are taught together.
misconceptions.correction: A liquid keeps a fixed volume, but a gas does not. Its molecules are far apart, so raising the pressure squeezes them into a smaller volume and lowering the pressure lets the gas expand.

misconceptions.question: A gas at 300 kPa in 0.020 m^3 expands to 0.150 m^3 at constant temperature. How is the new pressure found?
misconceptions.correct: Multiply 300 kPa by 0.020 m^3 and divide by 0.150 m^3, which gives a smaller pressure.
misconceptions.misconception: Multiply 300 kPa by 0.150 m^3 and divide by 0.020 m^3, which gives a larger pressure.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students substitute the numbers into a remembered ratio without asking which way the answer should go, so the volume ratio ends up inverted.
misconceptions.correction: Check the direction first: the gas has expanded, so the pressure must fall. Only p1 V1 ÷ V2 gives a smaller pressure; if the answer is bigger than the starting pressure, the ratio has been inverted.

misconceptions.question: A student writes 'pressure × volume = constant' and says it works for any gas in any situation. Is that right?
misconceptions.correct: No. The relationship only applies to a fixed mass of gas held at constant temperature. If gas is added or removed, or the temperature changes, the product p × V is no longer constant.
misconceptions.misconception: An equation given in physics is a universal law, so pV = constant works for any amount of gas whatever its temperature is doing — the conditions are just details of the original experiment.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Equations are practised as stand-alone formulas to substitute numbers into, so the conditions attached to a law are read as background about how it was discovered rather than as requirements for it to hold.
misconceptions.correction: Every gas law carries conditions. pV = constant compares two states of the same trapped sample of gas at the same temperature. Doubling the amount of gas, or letting it warm or cool, changes p × V, so the mass must be fixed and the temperature constant before the equation can be used.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the molecules of a gas is correct?

options.text: They are in constant random motion, and the temperature of the gas is related to their average kinetic energy.
options.rationale: This is what the specification states: the molecules of a gas are in constant random motion, and the temperature of the gas is related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules.

options.text: They are in constant random motion, and the temperature of the gas is set by their total kinetic energy.
options.rationale: The first half is right, which makes it tempting; students who know a bigger hot sample stores more energy swap 'average' for 'total'.

options.text: They all move at one single fixed speed, and the temperature of the gas is set by that shared speed.
options.rationale: Animations show identical particles moving identically, so 'random' is read as random direction only, with one speed for all.

options.text: They move along fixed repeating paths, and the temperature of the gas is set by their spacing.
options.rationale: Treats how far apart the molecules are, rather than how fast they move, as what temperature measures — the picture students hold of a hot gas as a spread-out one.

mcqs.stem: A sealed container of gas is heated and the temperature of the gas rises. What happens to the molecules of the gas?

options.text: They all speed up by exactly the same amount and keep sharing one common speed.
options.rationale: Keeps the idea of a single shared speed for every molecule, which survives because diagrams rarely show a spread of speeds.

options.text: Their average kinetic energy rises, so the molecules move faster on average.
options.rationale: The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its molecules, so raising the temperature raises that average and the molecules move faster on average.

options.text: Each molecule expands, so the gas now fills more of the container space.
options.rationale: Carries 'heating makes things bigger' from the thermal expansion of solids down to the particle scale.

options.text: They collide with one another less often, now that they have energy.
options.rationale: Sounds plausible if a student pictures energetic molecules escaping each other, but faster molecules in the same space collide more often, not less.

mcqs.stem: A fixed mass of gas is sealed in a rigid container, so its volume cannot change. The gas is then heated. What happens to the pressure the gas exerts?

options.text: It stays the same, because the trapped gas is not able to expand.
options.rationale: Links pressure changes to volume changes only, so a container that cannot move seems to rule out any change at all.

options.text: It falls, because the heated molecules swell and spread apart.
options.rationale: Combines 'heating makes particles bigger' with the idea that spacing sets the pressure; in a rigid container the molecules cannot spread out at all.

options.text: It increases, because the molecules hit the walls harder.
options.rationale: Changing the temperature of a gas held at constant volume changes the pressure exerted: the faster molecules strike the walls more often and with greater force.

options.text: It rises briefly, then falls back to its old value.
options.rationale: Assumes the gas 'settles' after heating, as students expect of a system returning to equilibrium; at the new steady temperature the higher pressure is maintained.

mcqs.stem: What causes the pressure that a gas exerts on the walls of its container?

options.text: The gas molecules repelling each other and pushing on the walls.
options.rationale: Students who have met electrostatic repulsion look for a force acting between particles at a distance to explain why a gas fills its container.

options.text: The weight of the gas above pressing down on the container.
options.rationale: Pressure is first taught with a block on a table, where the force really is a weight acting downwards, and that picture is carried over to gases.

options.text: The molecules swelling up and pressing against the walls.
options.rationale: Treats particle size, rather than particle motion, as the source of the push on the wall.

options.text: The molecules of the gas colliding with the walls of it.
options.rationale: Gas pressure comes from the huge number of collisions the randomly moving molecules make with the walls each second, each collision exerting a small force.

mcqs.stem: Two identical rigid sealed flasks hold the same gas. Flask X is kept at 20 °C and flask Y at 80 °C. Why is the pressure in flask Y higher?

options.text: The molecules in Y have swollen to a larger size, so they press harder on the walls.
options.rationale: Applies thermal expansion to the molecules themselves rather than to their motion.

options.text: The molecules in Y have a greater average kinetic energy, so they hit the walls harder.
options.rationale: The higher temperature means a higher average kinetic energy, so in the same fixed volume the collisions with the walls are both more frequent and more forceful.

options.text: The molecules in Y repel one another far more strongly at the higher temperature.
options.rationale: Keeps repulsion between molecules as the source of pressure and makes that repulsion depend on temperature.

options.text: The molecules in Y are packed more closely together than those in flask X.
options.rationale: The flasks are identical and sealed, so the same number of molecules occupies the same volume; spacing cannot be the difference.

mcqs.stem: A fixed mass of gas is cooled while its volume is kept constant. Using the particle model, what happens to the pressure of the gas?

options.text: It stays the same, because the rigid container will not let the gas shrink at all.
options.rationale: Assumes pressure can only change if the volume changes, so a rigid container seems to freeze the pressure.

options.text: It increases, because the cooled molecules move closer to the walls of it.
options.rationale: Borrows contraction on cooling from solids and liquids and treats closeness to the wall, rather than collision rate, as the cause of pressure.

options.text: It decreases, because slower molecules hit the walls less often and less hard.
options.rationale: Cooling lowers the average kinetic energy, so the molecules collide with the walls both less frequently and with less force, and the pressure falls.

options.text: It decreases, because the molecules shrink in size as the gas cools down.
options.rationale: Reaches the right direction by the wrong mechanism — particle size does not change with temperature.

mcqs.stem: The pressure of a gas produces a net force on the wall of its container. In which direction does that net force act?

options.text: At an angle that depends on the shape of the container.
options.rationale: Students expect a curved or slanted wall to change the direction of the push, rather than the orientation of the wall itself setting it.

options.text: Along the surface of the wall, in the direction of flow.
options.rationale: Pictures gas blowing past a surface like a wind, transferring that sideways push to a sealed container.

options.text: Straight down, because of the weight of the gas.
options.rationale: Treats gas pressure as a weight effect, so the force is expected to act downwards only.

options.text: At right angles to the surface of the container wall.
options.rationale: The specification states that the pressure produces a net force at right angles to the wall of the gas container, or any surface, because the sideways parts of the impacts cancel.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about a gas and changes of pressure is correct?

options.text: A gas can be compressed or expanded by pressure changes.
options.rationale: This is the specification statement: the molecules of a gas are far apart, so a change of pressure can squeeze the gas into a smaller volume or let it expand.

options.text: A gas keeps a fixed volume whatever pressure is applied to it.
options.rationale: Applies the rule learned for liquids — fixed volume, variable shape — to gases as well, since both are fluids.

options.text: A gas can be expanded by pressure changes but never compressed.
options.rationale: A halfway version of the same error: expansion is easy to picture, but students doubt that molecules can be pushed closer together.

options.text: A gas can only be compressed if it is squeezed from above.
options.rationale: Ties compression to a downward push, which follows from thinking of gas pressure as a weight acting downwards.

mcqs.stem: A fixed mass of gas is allowed to expand into a larger volume at constant temperature. Using the particle model, why does the pressure decrease?

options.text: Each molecule strikes the wall more gently, since it now has less kinetic energy.
options.rationale: Assumes that spreading out costs the molecules energy; at constant temperature the average kinetic energy is unchanged.

options.text: The molecules cool down as they spread out into the much larger space.
options.rationale: Ignores the stated condition of constant temperature and assumes that expansion must cool the gas.

options.text: The molecules travel further between wall collisions, so there are fewer collisions.
options.rationale: At constant temperature the molecules keep the same average speed, but in a larger volume each one takes longer to reach a wall, so the collision rate and the pressure both fall.

options.text: The molecules shrink in size once they are given more room to move about.
options.rationale: Uses particle size as the variable again, this time shrinking the molecules to explain a lower pressure.

mcqs.stem: Under which conditions does the relationship pressure × volume = constant apply to a gas?

options.text: Any mass of gas at all, whatever its temperature happens to be doing.
options.rationale: The relationship is memorised as a bare formula, with its conditions treated as background text rather than as part of the statement.

options.text: A fixed mass of gas whose temperature is steadily climbing.
options.rationale: Notices the 'fixed mass' condition but not the 'constant temperature' one, which is the condition students most often drop.

options.text: Any gas at all, so long as its container has been sealed.
options.rationale: A sealed container fixes the mass but says nothing about the temperature, so the product p V can still change.

options.text: A fixed mass of gas that is being held at a constant temperature.
options.rationale: The specification introduces the relationship with exactly this condition: for a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature, pressure × volume = constant.

mcqs.stem: For a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature, which relationship does the specification give?

options.text: pressure × volume = constant, written as [p V = constant]
options.rationale: This is the relationship exactly as the specification states it, together with the symbol form the specification gives in brackets.

options.text: pressure ÷ volume = constant, written as [p / V = a constant]
options.rationale: Comes from expecting a direct proportion, as in most earlier GCSE relationships, so p and V are written as a ratio.

options.text: pressure = volume × constant, written as [p = k V]
options.rationale: Another way of making 'constant' describe the pair rather than their product; adding two different quantities is not meaningful.

options.text: pressure × volume = temperature, written as [p V = T]
options.rationale: Recalls that temperature matters here and puts it into the equation, when in fact temperature is the condition that must be held constant.

mcqs.stem: Which units does the specification give for the two quantities in p V = constant?

options.text: Pressure in newtons, N, and volume in centimetres cubed, cm^3.
options.rationale: Uses the force unit for pressure, because pressure is introduced as a push, and keeps the laboratory unit for volume.

options.text: Pressure in pascals, Pa, and volume in metres cubed, m^3.
options.rationale: The specification states pressure, p, in pascals, Pa, and volume, V, in metres cubed, m^3.

options.text: Pressure in pascals, Pa, and volume in cubic centimetres, cm^3.
options.rationale: Volumes are usually measured in cm^3 in the laboratory, so students leave them unconverted.

options.text: Pressure in pascals, Pa, and volume in metres squared, m^2.
options.rationale: Carries the squared unit across from the area in the definition of pressure to the volume in the same equation.

mcqs.stem: A fixed mass of gas has a volume of 0.125 m^3 at a pressure of 80 kPa. At constant temperature the pressure is increased to 800 kPa. What is the new volume of the gas?

options.rationale: Reads 'constant' as meaning that the volume itself cannot change for a fixed mass, so the starting volume is given as the answer.
Multiplies by the pressure ratio instead of dividing by it, so the volume rises when the pressure rises.
Gives just the pressure ratio 800 ÷ 80, forgetting to bring the starting volume into the calculation.
p V = constant, so 80 × 0.125 = 800 × V, giving V = 10 ÷ 800 = 0.0125 m^3. The pressure is ten times larger, so the volume is ten times smaller.

mcqs.stem: A fixed mass of gas at a pressure of 300 kPa occupies 0.020 m^3. At constant temperature it is allowed to expand to 0.150 m^3. What is the new pressure of the gas?

options.text: 40 kPa
options.rationale: p V = constant, so 300 × 0.020 = p × 0.150, giving p = 6.0 ÷ 0.150 = 40 kPa. The gas has expanded, so the pressure must fall.

options.text: 300 kPa
options.rationale: Assumes that a fixed mass at constant temperature must also keep a constant pressure, so nothing is calculated.

options.text: 2250 kPa
options.rationale: Inverts the volume ratio, multiplying by 0.150 and dividing by 0.020, so the pressure rises even though the gas has expanded.
Reads 0.150 m^3 as 150, a unit slip of the kind that makes an answer wrong by a factor of a thousand.

mcqs.stem: In physics, what is meant by work?

options.text: Work is the energy stored inside a moving body.
options.rationale: Confuses work, which is a transfer, with the kinetic energy store that the transfer may fill.

options.text: Work is the transfer of energy by a force.
options.rationale: This is the specification statement: work is the transfer of energy by a force.

options.text: Work is a force acting over a given distance.
options.rationale: Describes work by the calculation met first, W = F s, so work is named as a force rather than as an energy transfer.

options.text: Work is the heating caused by a force.
options.rationale: Merges work with heating; the two are different ways of transferring energy, and a force need not produce any heating at all.

mcqs.stem: A cyclist uses a bicycle pump to inflate a tyre, and the barrel of the pump becomes noticeably warm. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Friction between the piston seal and the barrel is the only cause of the warming.
options.rationale: Friction is the familiar explanation for anything that warms up when it is moved, and the piston can be felt sticking.

options.text: Warm air is drawn in from outside, and that air heats the metal barrel.
options.rationale: Expects a temperature rise to require a hotter object, because every earlier example of heating involved a heat source.

options.text: Work is done on the gas as it is compressed, raising its internal energy.
options.rationale: The piston exerts a force that moves, so work is done on the enclosed gas. That transfer increases the internal energy of the gas and can cause its temperature to rise.

options.text: The gas loses internal energy as it is squeezed, so heat is released.
options.rationale: Pictures squeezing as forcing energy out, like water from a sponge, rather than as a transfer of energy into the gas.
